To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the C-terminal domain of the TraR, a member of the GntR family, functions in oligomerization and that the minimum region for oligomerization is the region from R95 to P150.
the TraR protein functions as a tetramer and that the CTD of TraR is responsible for the oligomerization of TraR protein.
the TraR repressor protein, which is classified in the HutC subfamly of the GntR protein, has two domains and that the C-terminal domain functions in oligomerization of TraR.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the function of the carboxyl-terminal domain of a repressor belonging to the HutC subfamilies of the GntR family.
the domain structure and oligomerization of TraR, which is a member of the HTH GntR protein subfamily.
the domain organization of the TraR repressor and its function in oligomerization.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the C-terminal region of TraR is involved in oligomerization, but the oligomeric state of TraR is still unknown.
the TraR protein is a tetramer, which functions to repress transcription of traR, traA, and traB by binding to the cis element in the tra operon promoter region.
the TraR protein is an oligomer that functions in DNA binding and repression of the tra operons.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the CTD of TraR is a domain for oligomerization, which is essential for repressor function.
the C-terminal domain of TraR is a tetramerization domain.
TraR functions as a tetramer and the CTD functions to form an active tetramer of TraR.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we have shown the domain structure of TraR and the role of the carboxyl-terminal region in oligomer formation.
the C-terminal domain of the TraR repressor is required for oligomer formation and is essential for its repressor function.
the CTD is involved in oligomerization and the formation of tetramers.
